Exercise
EK-ser-syze
n. / v.
From Latin exercere, to drive on, to keep busy, to train. Webster 1828: use; practice; the exertion of the body for health or amusement; and the discipline or training of the mind. Paul takes the gymnasium word and applies it to godliness and to the conscience.

Biblical Definition

Exercise in the New Testament is a training word, borrowed from the gymnasium and used of the soul. Paul’s charge to Timothy is the classic instance: refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness (1 Timothy 4:7), followed by the comparison of returns — bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things. He does not say bodily training is worthless; he says it profits a little and godliness profits in both worlds. The same word describes the maturing of discernment: strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil (Hebrews 5:14). Discernment is not a gift dropped on a Christian; it is a faculty trained by use, and the untrained believer is called a babe in the preceding verse. Hebrews uses it again of affliction: chastening yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11) — the trouble is the trainer. And Paul applies it to himself in Caesarea: herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men (Acts 24:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EXERCISE as use; practice; the exertion of the body for health, or of the mind in study; and, as a verb, to employ, to train, to discipline, to habituate to action. The Latin root means to drive on or keep at work.

expand to see more

EXERCISE, n. — Use; practice; the exertions and movements customary in the performance of business.

Practice; performance; as the exercise of religion, the exercise of an office.

Exertion of the body for health or amusement; also, the discipline and training of soldiers.

EXERCISE, v.t. — To employ; to exert; to train by use; to habituate to action; to discipline.

From Latin exercere, to drive on, keep busy — the same root as exercitus, an army, a body of men kept in training.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 4:7 — "But refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness."

1 Timothy 4:8 — "For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come."

Hebrews 5:14 — "But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil."

Hebrews 12:11 — "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby."

Acts 24:16 — "And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men."

Modern Corruption

Sanctification is presented in much modern teaching as something that happens to a passive believer, and 1 Timothy 4:7 answers with an imperative from the training ground: exercise thyself.

expand to see more

There is a genuine truth being defended by those who resist all talk of effort — that a man contributes nothing to his justification, and that sanctification is the work of the Spirit and not of the flesh. Scripture keeps both. Philippians 2 gives the command and the ground in consecutive verses: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. Paul’s word to Timothy is a gymnasium word, and it assumes repetition, discipline, and days when the thing is not enjoyable. The means are the ordinary ones the Reformed have always named: the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the Lord’s day, the fellowship of the saints. Nobody drifts into godliness.

Hebrews 5:14 removes the other excuse, which is the assumption that discernment is a temperament some Christians have. The senses are exercised to discern good and evil by reason of use, and the writer is rebuking a congregation that ought by this time to be teaching and still needs milk. A believer who cannot tell sound doctrine from plausible error is not suffering from a missing gift; he is untrained, and the training is available. Hebrews 12:11 then adds the part no one chooses: affliction is a trainer too, and the fruit it yields is peaceable but it comes afterward, which is the whole difficulty of enduring it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek gumnazo (G1128), to train naked in the gymnasium, whence the figure in 1 Timothy 4:7 and Hebrews 5:14; askeo (G778) at Acts 24:16, the root of ascetic.

expand to see more

Greek gumnazo (G1128) — to exercise, to train as an athlete; 1 Timothy 4:7, Hebrews 5:14, 12:11.

Greek gumnasia (G1129) — bodily exercise, training; a hapax legomenon at 1 Timothy 4:8.

Greek askeo (G778) — to practise, to exert oneself; only at Acts 24:16, and the root of ascetic.

Greek hexis (G1838) — habit, practice from long use; by reason of use (Hebrews 5:14).

Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness, piety; the object of the training in 1 Timothy 4:7-8.

Usage

"Exercise thyself rather unto godliness (1 Timothy 4:7) — the gymnasium word applied to the soul."

"By reason of use have their senses exercised (Hebrews 5:14) — discernment is trained, not issued."

"Them which are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11) — affliction as the trainer."
